parts:
Dear all,

This is an error message that has been commented previously. However, the answers it received did not help us. Simone Tenan and I have been trying for two days to adapt the jags code from a paper we wrote on estimating population growth rate from CR data in the hope to speed the calculations with Nimble and have a better understanding of what could be improved; It is using the zero trick and may be awkward. We tried different things to get around this nagging error message in vain. I specify  that we tried it on two different computers with different OS (Windows 10 and Linux Ubuntu), so it is unlikely to be related to the local implementation. The data are attached as an RData file and the R code that results in the error message follows:


### Towards Nimble  ##########
library(nimble)

### Derive data for JAGS ###
load("capsid_BUGS_data.RData")

DDCode <-  nimbleCode({
  ########### PRIORS #######################
  gamma[1] <- 0
  phi[s] <- 0
  # logit constraint for phi
  for (t in 1:(s-1)){
    phi[t] <- 1 / (1 + exp(-logit.phi[t]))
    logit.phi[t] <- mu.phi + eps.phi[t]
    eps.phi[t] ~ dnorm(0, tau.phi)
  }
  mu.phi <- log(mean.phi / (1-mean.phi))
  mean.phi ~ dunif(0,1)
  tau.phi <- 1 / (sigma.phi * sigma.phi)
  sigma.phi ~ dunif(0, 5)
  # log constraint for PGR
  for (t in 1:(s-1)){
    rho[t] <- exp(log.rho[t])
    log.rho[t] <- mu.rho + eps.rho[t]
    eps.rho[t] ~ dnorm(0, tau.rho)
  }
  mu.rho ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
  mean.rho <- exp(mu.rho)
  tau.rho <- 1 / (sigma.rho * sigma.rho)
  sigma.rho ~ dunif(0, 2)
  # logit constraint for p
  for (t in 1:s){
    p[t] <- 1 / (1 + exp(-logit.p[t]))
    logit.p[t] <- mu.p + eps.p[t]
    eps.p[t] ~ dnorm(0, tau.p)
    # no constraints for mu    
    mu[t] ~ dunif(0,1)
  }
  mu.p <- log(mean.p / (1-mean.p))
  mean.p ~ dunif(0,1)
  tau.p <- 1 / (sigma.p * sigma.p)
  sigma.p ~ dunif(0, 5)
  ########### LIKELIHOOD (ZERO-TRICK) ######
  zeros ~ dpois(zero.mean)
  zero.mean <- -L + C
  L <- sum(l.num[1:s]) - l.denom
  ##### log-likelihood for the first occasion
  l.num[1] <- (u[1] * log(xi[1])) + (n[1] * log(p[1])) + (secondexpo[1] * log(1-p[1])) +
   
 (thirdexpo[1] * log(phi[1])) + (fourthexpo[1] * log(mu[1])) + (d[1] *
log(1-mu[1])) + (fifthexpo[1] * log(1-(p[1]*(1-mu[1])))) +
    (sixthexpo[1] * log(chi[1]))
 
  xi[1] <- 1
  secondexpo_a[1] <- sum(u[1:1])
  secondexpo_b[1] <- 0
  secondexpo[1] <- secondexpo_a[1] - secondexpo_b[1] - n[1]
  thirdexpo[1] <- sum(v[2:s])
  fourthexpo[1] <- n[1]-d[1]
  fifthexpo[1] <- sum(u[2:s])
  sixthexpo[1] <- v[1]-d[1]
  ##### log-likelihood for the last occasion
 
 l.num[s] <- (u[s] * log(xi[s])) + (firstexpo[s] * (log(phi[s-1]) -
log(rho[s-1]))) + (n[s] * log(p[s])) + (secondexpo[s] * log(1-p[s])) +
    (fourthexpo[s] * log(mu[s])) + (d[s] * log(1-mu[s])) + (fifthexpo[s] * log(1-(p[s]*(1-mu[s])))) +
    (sixthexpo[s] * log(chi[s]))
  chi[s] <- 1
  firstexpo[s] <- sum(u[1:(s-1)])
  secondexpo_a[s] <- sum(u[1:s])
  secondexpo_b[s] <- sum(v[1:(s-1)])
  secondexpo[s] <- secondexpo_a[s] - secondexpo_b[s] - n[s]
  fourthexpo[s] <- n[s]-d[s]
  fifthexpo[s] <- 0
  sixthexpo[s] <- v[s]-d[s]
  ##### likelihood from occasion 2 to s-1
  for (i in 2:(s-1)) {
   
 l.num[i] <- (u[i] * log(xi[i])) + (firstexpo[i] * (log(phi[i-1]) -
log(rho[i-1]))) + (n[i] * log(p[i])) + (secondexpo[i] * log(1-p[i])) +
     
 (thirdexpo[i] * log(phi[i])) + (fourthexpo[i] * log(mu[i])) + (d[i] *
log(1-mu[i])) + (fifthexpo[i] * log(1-(p[i]*(1-mu[i])))) +
      (sixthexpo[i] * log(chi[i]))
    # first exponent
    firstexpo[i] <- sum(u[1:(i-1)])
    # second exponent
    secondexpo_a[i] <- sum(u[1:i])
    secondexpo_b[i] <- sum(v[1:(i-1)])
    secondexpo[i] <- secondexpo_a[i] - secondexpo_b[i] - n[i]
    # third exponent
    thirdexpo[i] <- sum(v[(i+1):s])
    # fourth exponent
    fourthexpo[i] <- n[i]-d[i]
    # fifth exponent
    fifthexpo[i] <- sum(u[(i+1):s])
    # sixth exponent
    sixthexpo[i] <- v[i]-d[i]
  }
  ##### likelihood denominator
  # 1st product
  PROD1[1] <- 1
  for (j in 1:(s-1)){
    PROD1_tmp[1,j] <- 0
  }
  # fill part of PROD1_tmp
  for (i in 2:(s-1)) {
    for (j in i:(s-1)){
      PROD1_tmp[i,j] <- 0
    }
  }
  for (i in 2:s) {
    for (j in 1:(i-1)){
      PROD1_tmp[i,j] <- phi[j] * (1-(p[j]*(1-mu[j])))
    }
  }
  PROD1[2] <- PROD1_tmp[2,1]
  for (i in 3:s) {
    PROD1[i] <- prod(PROD1_tmp[i,1:(i-1)])
  }
  # 2nd product
  PROD2[s] <- 1
  for (i in 1:(s-1)) {
    for (j in (i+1):s) {
      PROD2_tmp[i,j] <- gamma[j]
    }
  }
  # fill part of PROD2_tmp
  for (i in 1:(s-1)) {
    for (j in 1:i) {
      PROD2_tmp[i,j] <- 0
    }
  }
  PROD2[s-1] <- PROD2_tmp[(s-1),s]
  for (i in 1:(s-2)) {
    PROD2[i] <- prod(PROD2_tmp[i,(i+1):s])
  }
  for (i in 1:s) {
    denom_base_tmp[i] <- xi[i] * PROD1[i] * PROD2[i] * p[i]
  }
  denom_base <- sum(denom_base_tmp[1:s])
  denom_expo <- sum(u[1:s])
  l.denom <- denom_expo * log(denom_base)
  ################# Define xi and chi
  for (i in 2:s) {
    xi.tmp[i] <- (1-gamma[i]) + (gamma[i] * ((1-p[i-1])/(1-(p[i-1] * (1-mu[i-1])))) * xi[i-1])
    xi[i] <- max(xi.tmp[i],0.00001)
  }
  for (i in 1:(s-1)) {
    chi[i] <- (1-phi[i]) + (phi[i] * (1-p[i+1]) * chi[i+1])
  }
  ################# Gamma as derived parameter
  for (i in 2:s) {
    gamma[i] <- (phi[i-1] / rho[i-1])
    gamma_constr[i] <- min(gamma[i],1)
  }
}
)

inits <- function(){list(mean.phi = runif(1, 0.7, 0.9),sigma.phi=runif(1,0,1),
                         mu.rho = runif(1, 0.95, 1), sigma.rho = runif(1, 0, 1),
                         mean.p = runif(1, 0.6, 0.8),sigma.p=runif(1,0,1),
                         mu = runif(bugs.data$s, 0.3, 1)
)}

DD <- nimbleModel(DDCode,constants = list(C=10000,s=bugs.data$s),data = bugs.data[1:4], inits = inits())

CDD <- compileNimble(DD,showCompilerOutput = TRUE)

Unfortunately, nimbleFunctions with setup code can't be used in models.

One work-around is to embed the vectors you create in the setup code into the model itself.  Even if they aren't part of the model from a statistical point of view, putting them into the model makes it possible to pass them to a nimbleFunction used in the model. For example, you should be able to say

x ~ condL(phi[1:T], <other model variables>..., expos[1:8, 1:s])

Then set up the expos in R (To keep it short, I assumed you could pack the eight "expo" variables into a matrix, but you could keep them separate) and provide them to the model as data (or constants; it shouldn't matter).  They'll be passed to condL every time it is called.

Another option would be to use a nimbleExternalCall to call a C function you would write for condL.  In the C code you could arrange access to the constants ("expo" variables) you need.  

The run function will be a bit faster if you use numeric(length = s, init = FALSE) when you do not need to rely on initialization with zeros.  It was surprising, but I once clocked a noticeable performance improvement by avoiding unnecessary initialization.

-Perry
